extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and constraints for newspaper correspondents reporting from the Korean War front (security/censorship, military reporting rules, liaison practices, and treatment of enemy broadcasts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Army censorship authority
rubrics_metrics.description: “Lt. Gen. Walton H. Walker, Eighth Army commander has full power to impose censorship when or if he deems it necessary, he has not done so.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The army commander may impose censorship at his discretion. Although censorship had not been actively imposed at the time, correspondents must be aware that military authorities hold that power and that publication could be subject to retroactive restriction or sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondent's primary responsibility and judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: “Thus the primary responsibility still rests upon the correspondent himself. If he transmits news which the Army considers objectionable for security reasons, he has to answer for it.” and “MacArthur told the newsmen when he lifted the ban that he felt sound reporting rested on the almost intuitive judgment of trained newspapermen.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correspondents are expected to exercise their own judgment and responsibility in front-line reporting. Rely on trained professional judgment to balance newsworthiness and security concerns; be prepared to justify transmitted material to military authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to military regulations on naming wounded
rubrics_metrics.description: “Military regulations forbid using the names of wounded.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting from forward areas, do not publish the names of wounded personnel in violation of military regulations. This is a formal constraint—reporters should withhold names and comply with established military reporting rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow an internal code for correspondents and seek liaison
rubrics_metrics.description: “He also helped draw up a code for the correspondents' own use. He said he had suggested several times while in Korea that army authorities assign officers to work with field correspondents to guide and advise them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an internal code of conduct for battlefield reporting and, where possible, coordinate with assigned army officers or liaisons for guidance and security briefings. The piece notes that such liaison suggestions were made though not always implemented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish official communiques verbatim with timestamps/source
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple items present 'TEXT OF GENERAL MACARTHUR'S COMMUNIQUE' with specific issuance times (e.g., 'ISSUED AT 5340 P.M. (2340 G.M.T.)') and '(END TEXT)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial practice illustrated: republish full official communiques verbatim, clearly labeled and timestamped, and indicate the end of the quoted text. This preserves the official record and avoids paraphrase-errors for authoritative military statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat enemy broadcasts and prisoner statements with skepticism and context
rubrics_metrics.description: The article reproduces North Korean/Red China radio appeals (e.g., urging South Koreans to 'take up your guns against the Americans') and notes: 'Friends of Americans named as prisoners by the North Korean radio have insisted the soldiers would have made such statements only by coercion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting enemy propaganda or statements attributed to prisoners, present the broadcast content but clearly indicate potential coercion, lack of corroboration, or propaganda intent. Provide context and, where possible, statements from independent sources or friends/family to qualify authenticity.
